work_order.understanding:
Issue #19 asks for one browser-level test of the money path: create a group, add an expense with a remainder, read the balances, read the deterministic settlement, mark a transfer done, reload and confirm the state survived. It must run in CI, it must not add an npm dependency (ADR-0001), and it must exercise the BALANCES_INVARIANT 500 rather than stub around it.

What is missing is the seam, not the features. test/server.test.js already drives every route over a real socket and asserts the same numbers, so an HTTP-only test would prove nothing new. public/index.html carries real logic of its own — toPaise rejects '1,234' rather than recording ₹1.00, splitMemberIds is read from the checked checkboxes at submit time (index.html:455-456, against the `cb.checked = true` default at index.html:326), the two panels are re-read together from one snapshot, and a corrupt group is caught and rendered as one error line rather than a blank list (index.html:296-303). None of that is reached by any current test, because nothing runs the page.

The load-bearing constraint is therefore: drive a real browser with no package. That is possible with the standard library alone. Chrome's DevTools Protocol has a pipe transport (--remote-debugging-pipe) in which commands and responses are NUL-delimited JSON over the child's fd 3 and fd 4, which node:child_process exposes as ordinary socket streams. That needs no WebSocket client — which matters, because the global WebSocket only exists on Node 22+ and this product declares `engines: { node: ">=20" }` (ADR-0001).

Two things the proposal got wrong, both confirmed here by running them: the npm wiring it specified would have made CI red forever, and the checkbox-derived split it names as load-bearing was never actually varied. Both are corrected below.
work_order.approach:
Add a test-only browser driver and one e2e file. Change no product code: src/ and public/ are untouched, so nothing in the app can regress, and every line added is a line the next UI-to-domain refactor has to keep passing.

1. test/e2e/helpers/browser.js — the zero-dependency driver, plus a shared per-test app harness.
   - launchBrowser() resolves a Chrome binary (CHROME_PATH / CHROME_BIN first, then google-chrome, google-chrome-stable, chromium, chromium-browser, then the macOS app bundle), spawns it with --headless=new --disable-gpu --no-sandbox --disable-dev-shm-usage --remote-debugging-pipe and a mkdtemp'd --user-data-dir, and speaks CDP over the pipe. Stdio is ['ignore','pipe','pipe','pipe','pipe'] so fd 3 (write) and fd 4 (read) are the transport; messages are JSON terminated by \0; the reader is a Buffer that drains every complete message on each chunk. Commands are id-keyed promises; a CDP error rejects with the method name; the child's exit rejects anything still in flight so a crashed browser fails the test rather than hanging it. Exposes goto, reload, evaluate, close. evaluate uses Runtime.evaluate with awaitPromise and returnByValue and turns exceptionDetails into a thrown Error carrying the page's own message.
   - A page-side helper is installed with Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument, so it is defined before the app's own <script> and survives a reload: waitFor(fn, ms) polls on a 25ms timer and throws naming the condition on timeout; set(sel, value) assigns then dispatches input and change so the app's own listeners fire as they do for a user; click(sel); text(sel). All waiting is by polling for the expected condition, never a fixed sleep, so a slow machine fails on the assertion rather than passing by luck.
   - withApp(async ({ page, server, store }) => {}) — one helper that, per test: creates createStore({ memory: true }), starts the real server with start({ port: 0, store }), launches a browser, navigates to server.url, runs the body, and tears down browser then server in a finally. It exposes `store` because one test needs it (see test 3 below). Each test gets its own server, its own store and its own browser: no test inherits state, DOM or a recorded settlement from another, so a --test-name-pattern or t.only runs any single test correctly.
   - Money is compared by stripping ₹, commas and every whitespace variant (space, NBSP, narrow NBSP) **from the numeric part of a row only**; the member-name part is compared verbatim. The full-row strip the proposal specified is too loose — it would make two members whose names differ only in spacing compare equal, which is exactly the kind of regression this suite exists to catch. Names go in with textContent (index.html:229), so a name with an internal space is real text, not markup.
   - A comment in the helper records that the server resolves public/index.html against the current working directory, so the file must be run from the repository root — true under npm run sdlc:verify, false from anywhere else.

2. test/e2e/money-path.test.js — three tests, each self-contained behind withApp. Every value below was computed against this repository's real server during planning, and the three-way and two-way figures were re-derived independently here.

   Test 1 — the money path, the issue's six steps. Create 'Goa trip' with Asha, Rahul, Meera through #create-group-form, waiting for #group-title to read 'Goa trip'. Add ₹100 paid by Asha, split equally across all three through #expense-form (typed into the real inputs, payer from the real <select>, all three boxes left checked). 10000 paise over 3 shares: the expense card reads Asha ₹33.34, Rahul ₹33.33, Meera ₹33.33, summing back to the ₹100.00 on the same card — the extra paise goes to the first member in split order. Balances: Asha owed ₹66.66, Rahul owes ₹33.33, Meera owes ₹33.33, and the two sides are equal (summed in the test from the parsed rows, not hardcoded twice). Settlement: exactly two transfers, Rahul pays Asha ₹33.33 then Meera pays Asha ₹33.33 — the equal debtors broken by member-insertion order, which is what makes the settlement deterministic. Click the first .transfer-done-btn; both panels re-read together from one snapshot: Asha owed ₹33.33, Rahul even ₹0.00, Meera owes ₹33.33, one struck .transfer-done row and one pending transfer still carrying its button. Then reload and reopen: wait for #group-list to contain an li before clicking it (reload tears down the execution context, and clicking against a document that has not run loadGroups() selects nothing), wait for #group-title, and assert the same done-plus-pending panel. The store is the server's, so this is a real durability check across a full document teardown.

   Test 2 — the checkbox-derived split, which the issue's own argument rests on. Same setup, but uncheck Meera before submitting. 10000 paise over 2 shares: the card reads Asha ₹50.00 and Rahul ₹50.00 with no remainder, Meera owes ₹0.00, and the settlement is exactly one transfer, Rahul pays Asha ₹50.00 (a zero balance produces no transfer). This is the assertion that distinguishes index.html's submit-time read of `#split-checkboxes input:checked` from a hypothetical read of group.members — with all three boxes left checked, as the proposal had it, the two are indistinguishable and the test could not fail for the reason it exists.

   Test 3 — BALANCES_INVARIANT, exercised end to end. Build its own group and its own expense through the DOM, then corrupt it. The corruption is written through the MemoryStore instance withApp hands the test: load the groups, rewrite one expense's payerId to an id that is not a member, store.save(groups). There is no HTTP route that can do this and the implementer should not look for one — addExpense rejects a non-member payer at src/domain.js:81-83 with PAYER_UNKNOWN, a 400, so the store is the only way in. MemoryStore.save deep-copies (src/store.js:51), so the mutation is safe and does not leak into the running server's state. Then reload, reopen the group, and assert: #balances-error carries the server's own message, #balances-list is empty, #expense-list still renders the corrupt group's expenses. And also, per the same single failure — both endpoints 500, /balances and /settlement, by design (src/server.js:226) — #settlement-list is empty and #settlement-error is empty. That second half is written as a **characterisation** assertion with a comment saying it is current behaviour and not a chosen contract: the Promise.all rejection writes to exactly one element, so a user with corrupt data sees a red line under Balances and an unlabelled, message-free Settlement panel beneath it. Whether that empty panel is itself a UX bug is left visible here, not settled by this test.

3. package.json — sdlc:verify becomes 'node --test test/*.test.js && node --test test/e2e/*.test.js', and a new sdlc:e2e runs the second half alone. sdlc:serve, sdlc:seed and sdlc:ready are unchanged and no dependencies field appears.
   Two deliberate differences from the proposal, both because node does not accept a directory as a positional test argument (reproduced here: `node --test test/e2e/` reports `not ok 1 - test/e2e`, `# fail 1`, and the whole chain exits 1 on every run with correct code).
   - The e2e half names a file glob, not the directory. It is left **unquoted** on purpose. Quoting it works only because node grew glob support for positional test args in v22.6.0, and the product supports Node 20 (engines >=20) — the same Node 20 support that is the entire reason for choosing the pipe transport over the WebSocket endpoint. An unquoted `test/e2e/*.test.js` is expanded by sh, which every POSIX shell has always done, and the result is a plain file path that every Node version accepts.
   - `--test-concurrency=1` is **dropped**. It was added in Node 21.0.0 and backported only to v20.10.0, so on Node 20.0–20.9 — versions this package's engines field admits — it is a hard `bad option` failure before any test runs. It buys nothing here regardless: node runs a file's tests sequentially in one process, and there is one e2e file, so one Chrome at a time already holds without the flag. (It would also only have limited concurrency between files, not between tests within one file.)
   Narrowing bare `node --test` to the two explicit globs is load-bearing, not cosmetic: node treats every .js under a directory named test as a test file, so under today's script the new helper reports `ok 1 - test/e2e/helpers/browser.js` — a suite that never launched a browser, green. These two edits must land together; if the package.json change is dropped or reverted, the helper goes back to reporting a pass.
   Because verify.unit in .sdlc/config.yml is 'npm run sdlc:verify', this script is the only lever that puts the suite in CI — .github/** and .sdlc/config.yml are both forbidden to this plan, so verify.e2e stays empty and the suite runs inside the unit check. That is the 'as part of sdlc:verify' branch the issue explicitly allows.

4. README.md — a short note that the e2e suite needs a Chrome or Chromium binary, that CHROME_PATH (or CHROME_BIN) overrides the lookup, and that the assertions pin the exact 'owed' / 'owes' / 'even' wording in the balances panel (public/index.html:230-231) and the 'X pays Y ₹N' / 'X paid Y ₹N (done)' wording in the settlement panel, so renaming a label is a test failure by design. Without the first line the failure is a bare ENOENT from spawn; without the second, the next person to edit that copy learns it from a red CI run instead of from the README.

qa_script: Run `npm run sdlc:verify` from the repository root and confirm it runs the unit files and then test/e2e/, that both halves report, and that the command exits 0. Record the exit code. Chrome boot is about a second, so the whole thing should be well under a minute. This step is not optional: the previous plan specified a command that exited 1 on every run and the only way that was caught was by someone running it.
Confirm the suite fails loudly rather than skipping: `CHROME_PATH=/nonexistent/chrome node --test test/e2e/*.test.js` must exit non-zero with the binary path in the message, not report a pass.

Drive the app by hand at http://localhost:3000 through the same path the test drives — create a group, add ₹100 split three ways, read balances, mark a transfer done, reload — and confirm the numbers the test asserts are what a person sees. The test should be a description of the app, not a description of itself.

Confirm the unchecking case by hand too: in the same group add a second ₹100 expense with one member's split box unchecked, and check the card reads ₹50.00 / ₹50.00 and the settlement gains a single Rahul → Asha ₹50.00 transfer.

Confirm the app is unchanged in the browser: no console errors on load, the group list and both panels render as before, and data/groups.json is written exactly as it was — the e2e uses an in-process MemoryStore and must not have created or touched data/.

Confirm the browser helper is not being reported as a test: the unit half's output must list the five existing files and nothing named browser.js. If a line called 'ok ... browser.js' appears, the package.json narrowing did not land.
risks: Chrome must exist on the machine running the suite. It was verified present here (/usr/bin) and the whole path was driven through it, but whether the GitHub ubuntu-latest runner image ships one could not be checked from this environment. If it does not, the suite fails with a message naming CHROME_PATH rather than passing quietly — a silent skip would mean CI quietly stopped testing the seam, which is the outcome this issue exists to prevent. The cost is that a contributor with no browser cannot run the full sdlc:verify; they can run `node --test test/*.test.js` for the unit half, and the README now says so.

The package.json edit and the helper's location under test/ are load-bearing for each other and must land together. node treats every .js under a directory named test as a test file, so if the narrowing to `test/*.test.js` and `test/e2e/*.test.js` is dropped or conflicts during review, the helper silently reports 'ok' beside the real tests and a suite that never launched a browser looks green.

sdlc:verify is the single gating command: ci-verify runs it as the unit step, verify-is-real.mjs inspects it beforehand, and the framework's gate reduces to that job's exit code. Editing it is a wider change than adding a test file, and this plan does it because it is the only lever available — .sdlc/config.yml and .github/** are both forbidden.

A browser failure will be reported as a unit-test failure, because the suite runs inside the command whose workflow step is named 'Unit tests'. A missing Chrome, a --no-sandbox refusal or a pipe-framing change produces a red check labelled unit with a browser error in it, pointing whoever reads the red PR at the wrong file. This is unavoidable given the forbidden paths and is the cost of the routing, not a mistake in it.

The driver talks CDP over the pipe transport, a less-travelled surface than the WebSocket endpoint. It has been stable for years and is what Puppeteer itself falls back to, but a Chrome upgrade that changed the pipe framing would break the driver rather than the app. The failure would be immediate and legible — every test in the file fails on its first command — not silent.

Clicks are dispatched with element.click() and fields are set by value assignment plus a real input/change event, rather than with synthesized OS-level key and mouse events. Everything the app does on a click runs for real — the listener, the fetch, the store, the domain — but the browser's own hit-testing and key handling are not under test. That is the right trade for a zero-dependency suite: those are the browser's to get right. A deliberate gap, not an oversight.

The assertions are coupled to the wording of renderBalances and renderSettlement ('owed' / 'owes' / 'even', 'X pays Y ₹N', 'X paid Y ₹N (done)'), so a copy edit makes the suite red with no behavioural change. Correct for a regression test, and the README now says so next to the CHROME_PATH note rather than leaving it in a plan document that will not be in the repo.

Headless Chrome writes dbus and sandbox warnings to stderr on a machine without a session bus. They are noise, not failures, and the driver never asserts on stderr — but they will appear in CI logs and should not be mistaken for a problem.
out_of_scope: A second money path. The issue is explicit that this is one load-bearing path and that more can come later. The unchecking case (AC-11) is the same path with one box off, not a new one.

Empty and single-member groups: the 'No expenses yet.', 'No balances yet.' and 'No settlements yet.' placeholder branches (index.html:207-209, 240-242, 368-371) stay unasserted. They are covered at the HTTP layer and nowhere else. This is a real gap and it is recorded in residual_risks, but adding a second path is the issue's call, not this plan's.

Double-submit and the in-flight guards (index.html:162-167, 544-548). The suite clicks once. Those guards are the seam most likely to be broken by a later refactor, and pinning them costs one extra click — but it is a different question from the one this issue asks.

Non-ASCII group and member names. The textContent-not-innerHTML escaping path is covered at the HTTP layer by xss.test.js; driving it in a browser with content that must be escaped is a reasonable later ticket.
Visual or responsive regression testing, and every other view and form. The by-shares split mode and the error paths (duplicate group name, bad amount, no members selected) are out of scope.
Coverage of the existing 149 unit tests in the browser. They stay where they are.

Filling verify.e2e in .sdlc/config.yml, and adding a named CI step beside sdlc:verify. Both files are forbidden to this plan, so the suite runs inside sdlc:verify — the other branch the issue allows. Recorded rather than routed around: if a human later wants a separate e2e job, it is a two-line config change they can make themselves.

Touching src/ or public/. Nothing in this ticket changes how the app behaves — including the empty settlement panel that AC-8 pins as characterised behaviour. If that panel turns out to be a UX bug, it is its own ticket against public/index.html.

alternatives_considered.approach: Playwright or Puppeteer, driving a real browser the conventional way.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It breaks ADR-0001 and the brief's invariant that a dependency is an architecture-level change: a package.json with a dependencies field is a different repository. It also makes the suite depend on an install step CI runs with --ignore-scripts, and on downloading a browser build, so a network hiccup becomes a red PR. The issue named this risk explicitly and asked for a choice that either justifies breaking the rule or avoids it. This avoids it, with a driver small enough for a maintainer to read in full.

alternatives_considered.approach: Drive Chrome over the DevTools Protocol's WebSocket endpoint (--remote-debugging-port) with Node's global WebSocket.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The global WebSocket does not exist on Node 20, which is what package.json engines and ADR-0001 promise. Using it means either raising the minimum Node version — a product decision nobody asked for — or hand-rolling an RFC 6455 client, which is more code and more risk than the pipe transport for no benefit. The pipe transport is the same protocol in NUL-delimited JSON over two fds, and node:child_process hands those over directly.

alternatives_considered.approach: The proposal's wiring, or the critique's replacement for it: 'node --test --test-concurrency=1 test/e2e/', or the same with the glob quoted so node expands it.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The directory form exits 1 on every run (reproduced here) and node only learned to expand globs in positional test args in v22.6.0, so the quoted form would break on the Node 20 the product declares support for — the very support that motivated the pipe transport. An unquoted 'test/e2e/*.test.js' is expanded by sh, which every POSIX shell has always done, and reaches node as a plain file path. Dropping --test-concurrency removes the last Node-20-incompatible token and costs nothing, since one e2e file already runs in one sequential process.

alternatives_considered.approach: No browser: a hand-rolled minimal DOM in the test, with the page's own inline script extracted from public/index.html and executed against it.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is not a browser test, and the issue's whole argument is that the UI-to-domain seam is unverified. A DOM shim tests a reimplementation of the browser's behaviour, so a real regression in fetch, event dispatch or rendering passes. It also duplicates the inline <script> into the test process, where it is a second copy of code that can drift. The version that survives a refactor is the one that runs the shipped file.

alternatives_considered.approach: An HTTP-only integration test covering the same six steps with fetch, asserting on API responses.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: test/server.test.js already does this, over a real socket, against the same routes and the same domain. It would add runtime and assertions without adding coverage, and it would leave the seam the issue actually names untouched, since toPaise, the checkbox-derived split list, the paired panel refresh and the corrupt-group error line all live in public/index.html, which no HTTP test runs.

alternatives_considered.approach: A shell script that seeds data and asserts on responses, with the browser left to QA.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: That is what the pipeline already does. The QA environment is fully wired and has no tests to run; a script QA reads once and reruns by hand is not a regression test, and it does not survive a refactor as a test does. The issue asks for something that fails loudly in CI when anything in the seam breaks.

assumptions: The GitHub ubuntu-latest runner image ships a Chrome or Chromium binary. This could not be checked from the planning environment. The lookup covers google-chrome, google-chrome-stable, chromium and chromium-browser plus the macOS bundle, and CHROME_PATH overrides all of them, but if none is present the suite fails rather than skips.

Chrome's --remote-debugging-pipe transport still frames commands and responses as NUL-delimited JSON on fds 3 and 4 in current Chrome versions. Verified against the Chrome installed here; a Chrome upgrade that changed it would break every test in the file immediately and legibly. Unlike the npm wiring, this was not independently re-run during arbitration — it rests on the proposer's report.

Running the app server in-process from a node:test file works and the browser can reach it — same origin, so the page's relative fetch('/api/groups') resolves against the ephemeral port. start({port:0, store}) returns { close, url } and the ephemeral port is in that url.

The MoneyStore-backed server keeps state in the server process for the life of the test, so a page reload genuinely tests durability rather than a re-seed. This follows from MemoryStore. Worth stating: the reload test proves the browser re-fetches, not that data/groups.json survives a restart. Disk persistence is store.test.js's job.

The corruption written in test 3 goes through the MemoryStore instance the test holds. There is no HTTP route that permits it — addExpense rejects a non-member payer with PAYER_UNKNOWN, a 400 (src/domain.js:81-83) — so this is the only mechanism available. MemoryStore.save deep-copies (src/store.js:51), so the mutation is safe and does not leak into the running server's state.

Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', INR) renders rupee amounts in a headless Chrome. The assertions strip the symbol, commas and all whitespace from the numeric part, so a different ICU build cannot break them; a locale change that reordered the number itself would.

npm runs scripts through sh on this platform, which expands the unquoted 'test/*.test.js' and 'test/e2e/*.test.js' globs. Both are single-level and need nothing beyond POSIX sh. 'test/*.test.js' is the complete set of unit files today (domain, money, server, store, xss — verified 149 tests, all passing), so the explicit glob does not silently drop a test; a future test in a subdirectory of test/ would need it widened.

No file outside test/, package.json and README.md is touched. In particular .sdlc/memory/**, docs/spec/**, .github/** and .sdlc/** are untouched, which is what keeps the guard from refusing the plan — verify.e2e in .sdlc/config.yml is left empty for exactly that reason, and that is stated in out_of_scope rather than worked around.
unknowns: Whether the CI runner has a Chrome binary, and which. Unresolvable from this environment and the single largest unknown in the plan; also the one whose failure is loudest and cheapest to fix.

Whether the CDP pipe driver works end to end. The proposers report having built and run the whole path in a real headless Chrome, and the critic independently reproduced every number the plan asserts over HTTP, but the driver itself was not re-run during arbitration. It is the one genuinely load-bearing piece resting on a single report.

Whether an empty, message-free settlement panel beside a corrupt-data error (AC-8) is the intended UX or a bug. This plan pins current behaviour and does not settle it, because settling it would mean editing public/index.html, which is out of scope here. If it is a bug, the test is where it should surface and the ticket is its own.

Whether whoever reviews this would rather the browser suite skip than fail on a machine with no browser. This plan chose fail, because a green suite that tested nothing is the specific failure this issue exists to prevent — but it is a call worth confirming, and the alternative is a t.skip() with a warning, which costs the guarantee.

How long the whole e2e file takes in CI. Chrome boot plus the steps measured at a couple of seconds here, but three tests with three browser launches have not been timed under the ci-verify job's conditions or on a loaded runner.
residual_risks: The empty-state and single-member branches ('No expenses yet.', 'No balances yet.', 'No settlements yet.') are unverified in a browser. They are covered at the HTTP layer and nowhere else. Deliberate — the issue asks for one path — but nobody should read this plan as the UI being covered.

The settlement panel's blank-on-corrupt-data half is characterised, not endorsed. If a reader assumes the test implies that behaviour is correct, the test has been misread; the comment in the file is the place that disambiguates.

The browser's own input handling — hit-testing, focus, keyboard — is not under test, because the suite dispatches DOM events rather than synthesized OS-level input. The app's handlers all run; the browser's plumbing does not.
The in-flight submit guards and the by-shares split mode are untouched, in a browser or anywhere new.
Only one browser engine is covered, and only headless. If the UI ever depends on engine-specific behaviour, this suite will not find it.

The e2e failures surface under a CI step labelled 'Unit tests', so a browser problem is reported in a place a reader is not looking for one. QA: read the residual risks here first, then the red step's log for anything mentioning chrome, CDP or a spawn ENOENT before assuming a domain regression.
work_order.confidence_rationale: The approach is sound and the hard part — whether a browser can be driven with no package — is answered with a mechanism that exists in Chrome and in Node's standard library, not a guess. Every number the plan asserts was independently recomputed during arbitration against this repository's real server: the three-way split (3334/3333/3333, balances 6666/-3333/-3333, settlement Rahul→Asha then Meera→Asha) and the two-way split (5000/5000, Meera 0, a single Rahul→Asha transfer), plus the 149-test baseline and the BALANCES_INVARIANT 500 from both /balances and /settlement. The one defect that would have shipped — an npm script that exits 1 forever — was found by the critique, reproduced here, and is now fixed and re-verified end to end at exit 0. What holds this below the 80s: the CDP pipe driver itself was never independently re-run, by me or by the critic, so one genuinely load-bearing component rests on a single report; the three-way glob form was exercised in a scratch tree, not in this repository with a real browser in it; and whether the GitHub runner image ships a Chrome cannot be checked from here. What would move it up: one run of `npm run sdlc:verify` on this repository with the driver in place, recording exit 0. What would move it down: a Node 20 box, or a runner image without a browser. The number is honest about being unverified wiring rather than a wrong diagnosis.
work_order.debate_summary:
The critique was right about one thing that mattered and I reproduced it before accepting it: `node --test` does not accept a directory as a positional argument. `node --test --test-concurrency=1 test/e2e/` reports `not ok 1 - test/e2e` and the proposed sdlc:verify chain exits 1 on every run with correct code. The proposal had recorded that as a verified assumption, which is the more serious half — the plan's headline confidence rested its entire CI guarantee on a command nobody had run. That is folded in, and AC-7 now requires `npm run sdlc:verify` to be run end to end with the exit code recorded, because that is the only check that covers the wiring.

I did not simply apply the critique's fix. The critique proposed quoting the glob so node expands it, on the grounds that node gained glob support in v22.6.0. That is correct for Node 22 and wrong for this product: package.json declares engines >=20 and the proposal's entire reason for choosing the pipe transport over the WebSocket endpoint was that Node 20 has no global WebSocket. A quoted glob would have reintroduced on the wiring the exact Node 20 incompatibility the driver was chosen to avoid. The work order uses an unquoted `test/e2e/*.test.js` — expanded by sh, delivered to node as a plain path, correct on both. On the same reasoning I dropped `--test-concurrency` rather than keeping it, since it does not exist below Node 20.10 and buys nothing with one e2e file. Both the proposal's version and the critique's version would have been red or version-dependent; neither was right.

The critique's two 'major' test findings are both correct and both folded in. It is right that a test leaving all three split boxes checked cannot distinguish the submit-time read of `#split-checkboxes input:checked` from a read of group.members — and the proposal had named that read as load-bearing in its own understanding. I computed the two-way numbers against the real server rather than taking them from the critique: Asha ₹50.00, Rahul ₹50.00, Meera ₹0.00, settlement exactly one transfer Rahul pays Asha ₹50.00. And it is right that the invariant test was silently coupled to the main test, with the undeclared mechanism being a direct write to the MemoryStore, since addExpense rejects a non-member payer at src/domain.js:81-83 and no route can persist the corruption. Every test now gets its own store, server and browser behind withApp, and the work order says in terms that the corruption is written through the store, so the implementer does not go looking for an HTTP route that cannot exist.

The settlement-panel finding is also correct and I verified both halves myself: the server returns BALANCES_INVARIANT from /settlement as well as /balances (src/server.js:226, deliberately), and loadBalancesAndSettlement writes the error to #balances-error only, leaving #settlement-list empty and #settlement-error untouched (index.html:296-303). It is now pinned as a characterisation assertion with a comment saying it is current behaviour rather than a chosen contract, and the open question sits in unknowns rather than being quietly closed by a test that blesses it.

The minor findings were all true: the helper really is reported as a passing test file under bare `node --test` (I reproduced `ok 1 - test/e2e/helpers/browser.js`), and the unit count is 149, not the 135 inherited from the issue text. Both folded in, the first as a risk that the two edits must land together. I took the critique's point on the whitespace strip as well — stripping across a whole row is right for money and quietly wrong for names — and specified stripping the numeric part only, comparing member names verbatim.

What I dismissed is the critique's list of missed edge cases beyond the corruption mechanism it identified: empty and single-member groups, the double-submit guards, non-ASCII names. These are real gaps and I have put them in out_of_scope and residual_risks so they are decisions rather than oversights, but adding them would widen a ticket the issue explicitly scoped to one path, and the arbiter's job is to decide the work order, not to enlarge the ticket. The critique's regression risks about the e2e suite reporting under a step named 'Unit tests', and about narrowing node's discovery, are accepted as stated rather than dismissed: the first is unavoidable given that .sdlc/config.yml and .github/** are forbidden, the second costs nothing today but is now written down.

Where the two disagree, the disagreement is only about wiring. The critique's verdict was 'flawed', not 'wrong-diagnosis', and I agree with that characterisation: the root cause — the seam is untested because nothing runs the page, and it can be run with no dependency — is right, and every number in it survives independent recomputation. I would put confidence higher than the proposal's own 82 only if the pipe driver had been re-run by someone other than the person who wrote it. It has not, and that is the honest gap in this plan.

history.action: route plan -> implement -> review -> qa (model, confidence 82)
